summary:
North Korea's Criminal Code of 1950, revised in 2009, appears to contain no penalty for consensual same-sex acts. Two provisions nonetheless leave enforcement to official discretion. Article 193 bans the import, keeping and distribution of "decadent culture", including sexual recordings, and Article 262 bans collective "obscene activities". Neither is defined in terms that constrain how it is applied. The US State Department's 2022 human rights report reaches the same conclusion, that no specific law criminalises same-sex conduct, and adds that the regime's total control leaves no space for LGBT life.

Official hostility runs alongside official denial. In April 2014 the state news agency KCNA rejected the UN Commission of Inquiry's report on the country as a political fabrication and attacked commissioner Michael Kirby as "a disgusting old lecher with a 40-odd-year-long career of homosexuality". The regime denies that homosexuality exists in the country while punishing it.

A 2023 South Korean Ministry of Unification report, the 584-page North Korean Human Rights Report, cites defector testimony that at least one male detainee in a detention camp was secretly executed for homosexuality in 2014. A 2011 Korea Times report attributed to Free North Korea Radio claimed the state executed a lesbian couple, a North Korean woman and a Japanese woman, for being influenced by capitalism and "bringing corruption of public morals". Both accounts rest on defector or exile testimony and have not been independently confirmed.

No North Korean law prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and the State Department states that the concepts do not appear in the legal system. The Constitution, last revised in 2024, does not address such discrimination. There is no registration route for LGBTI organisations. Outright International records no documented state or non-state violence against LGBTIQ people, a finding that sits alongside the executions reported above and reflects the near-total absence of information rather than a protective environment.

As of 2026 no North Korean law recognises same-sex marriage, civil unions or domestic partnerships. Article 8 of the Family Law provides that "Marriage may be done only between one man and one woman". A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under birth-sex status has no route to recognition, and the State Department's 2020 report records that same-sex couples could not legally adopt children.

Changing a sex marker on a birth certificate or citizen card is technically possible under "unavoidable circumstances", by application to the People's Security Agency with a state forensic medical evaluation; in practice the procedure requires surgical intervention. No law explicitly bans gender-affirming care, but the under-resourced health system makes hormones and surgery effectively inaccessible.

Newer statutes, among them the Pyongyang Cultural Protection Act, have tightened control in the decade since the UN Commission of Inquiry reported. A novelist who left the country in the late 1990s and was forcibly outed became the first publicly known gay defector, and an openly gay defector published an autobiography in 2017. CNN recorded in April 2017 a defector's account of homosexuality's place in North Korean society and of the punishment it carries.
tangentialFactors:
The two Criminal Code provisions that bear on sexual minorities are general censorship instruments rather than identity offences. Article 193's ban on importing, keeping or distributing "decadent culture", including sexual recordings, and Article 262's ban on collective "obscene activities" reach sexual content and gatherings broadly. Their significance for a trans visitor lies in the discretion they leave officials, not in any defined prohibition on status or conduct.

The legal order contains no category of sexual orientation or gender identity at all. There is therefore no protective framework to invoke and no administrative body with a mandate over such complaints; any redress would run through the same agencies that enforce the censorship provisions.

outOfScopeNotes:
The 2011 claim that a lesbian couple was executed rests on a single report in a South Korean newspaper attributed to Free North Korea Radio, an exile broadcaster, and has not been corroborated.

The 2014 detention-camp execution rests on defector testimony cited in a South Korean government report. No independent confirmation exists.

The State Department's 2020 report states that no reliable information on LGBT persons in North Korea is available. The country permits no independent human rights monitoring, so the scope and consistency of enforcement against trans and LGB people cannot be verified from outside.

Because Articles 193 and 262 are undefined, how they are applied in practice, and whether they are applied to trans visitors at all, is not documented.
